footer.tagline: LeanCTX is the Cognitive Context Layer for AI coding tools. It compresses what your AI reads, remembers context across sessions, and controls what reaches the model.
howItWorks.ctaDesc: One binary. Zero cloud dependencies. Apache-2.0 licensed. Install in 60 seconds and start saving tokens immediately.
howItWorks.archCtaDesc: Explore the Cognitive Context Layer: the six-step pipeline, integration modes, agent matrix, Context Field Theory, and nine architectural pillars that make LeanCTX work.
howItWorks.dataFlowDesc: LeanCTX intercepts at two levels: the context layer (file reads, code search, shell commands) and the shell layer (raw CLI output). Both compress data before it reaches the LLM. The AI sees the same information in a fraction of the tokens.
howItWorks.archDiagramDesc: Every capability runs inside a single Rust binary. Here is how a request flows through LeanCTX — from your AI tool, through the cognitive pipeline, to the model.
howItWorks.faq1A: LeanCTX is an open-source context layer for AI coding tools. It sits between your AI tool (Cursor, Claude Code, GitHub Copilot, etc.) and the LLM, helping agents compress, remember, and route context through AST-aware file compression, shell output pattern matching, and communication protocols. It reduces token usage by up to 99% per operation.
howItWorks.faq2A: No. LeanCTX uses tree-sitter AST parsing to understand code structure, then strips only what the LLM doesn't need: redundant whitespace, boilerplate imports, and decorative comments. On average, 98% of AST structure, 97% of identifiers, and 96% of meaningful code lines are preserved. You can verify this with lean-ctx benchmark run.
howItWorks.faq3A: Install via cargo install lean-ctx or curl -fsSL https://leanctx.com/install.sh | sh. Then run lean-ctx init for the shell hook and lean-ctx setup to connect with your AI tools. Zero configuration required.
howItWorks.faq4A: LeanCTX works with every major AI coding tool: Cursor, GitHub Copilot, Claude Code, Windsurf, Cline, OpenAI Codex, Gemini CLI, Antigravity, Pi, Crush, Zed, Continue, and OpenCode. All tools benefit from both the context server and shell hook compression.

howItWorks.securityPathJail: PathJail - All file operations are sandboxed to the project root. Symlink traversal, ../ escapes, and absolute paths outside the jail are blocked at the resolve_path chokepoint.

howItWorks.securityToctou: Safe file access - File reads can't be tricked into following symlinks out of your project, and the local proxy only ever talks to your own machine.

index.heroSubline: LeanCTX is one small Rust binary that perceives, compresses, remembers, routes, and governs every token between your AI and your codebase — automatically. Install it once: 60–90% fewer tokens per read, memory that survives across sessions, and guardrails on every tool call.
index.faq1A: LeanCTX is an open-source context layer for AI coding agents. It sits between your AI tool — Cursor, Claude Code, OpenAI Codex, GitHub Copilot, and 24+ others — and the model, automatically compressing file reads, shell output, and search results so the agent spends far fewer tokens (up to 99% less on large operations) without losing the signal it needs.
index.faq2Q: Does compressing context hurt answer quality?
index.faq2A: No. LeanCTX removes redundancy, not meaning: AST-aware file maps preserve signatures and structure, shell patterns keep the lines that matter (errors, results, diffs), and anything an agent later needs in full is re-expanded and netted out. The numbers in `lean-ctx gain` are the realized savings after those re-reads.
index.faq3A: One command, then one setup. Install via the script, Homebrew, npm, or cargo and run `lean-ctx setup` — LeanCTX auto-detects your editors and wires up the right hooks and MCP server for each. Upgrades are a single `lean-ctx update`.
index.faq4Q: Is any of my code or data sent to a server?
index.faq4A: No. Compression, caching, the savings ledger, and project memory all run locally on your machine — nothing is uploaded. The only network features (the Wrapped share card and the public leaderboard) are strictly opt-in and publish just an anonymous, whitelisted aggregate: a token count and a display name you choose.
index.faq5Q: Which AI tools does it work with?
index.faq5A: 24+ and growing — Cursor, Claude Code, OpenAI Codex, GitHub Copilot, Zed, Windsurf, Cline, Roo Code, Gemini CLI, OpenCode, and any MCP-capable client. LeanCTX integrates through native hooks where a tool supports them and through a standard MCP server everywhere else.

pillar.smartIo.title: Smart I/O
pillar.smartIo.headline: Your AI wastes 90% of its token budget reading files it doesn't need.
pillar.smartIo.solution: LeanCTX reads, compresses, and caches every file access through a 4-layer compression engine with quality gate. Choose from 10 intelligent read modes (from full cached reads to entropy-filtered signatures), leverage 95+ shell compression patterns for tools like git, npm, and docker, and use deterministic search with stable results. Every read is graph-aware: the Property Graph scores related files so the agent always knows what to read next. Re-reads cost as little as 13 tokens thanks to intelligent caching.

pillar.smartIo.feature2Desc: 95+ patterns for git, npm, cargo, docker and more. 60-90% smaller output, zero configuration.

pillar.smartIo.feature4Desc: Atomic writes with preimage guards, TOCTOU protection, and diff evidence.

pillar.smartIo.feature6Desc: Git-diff-based graph updates patch only changed nodes and edges instead of rebuilding the full graph.

pillar.intelligence.title: Intelligence
pillar.intelligence.headline: Your AI agent picks the wrong tools, ignores budgets, and wastes compute on trivial tasks.
pillar.intelligence.solution: LeanCTX routes every request through a graph-powered adaptive pipeline. It classifies task intent, fuses BM25 (pre-allocated score arrays), HNSW-indexed dense embeddings, and graph proximity via Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF) for search. Multi-scale indexing (micro/meso/macro) routes queries to the optimal granularity. Attention-weighted context assembly prioritizes information-dense results. Hebbian co-access caching with homeostatic memory management keeps long sessions efficient.

pillar.intelligence.feature2Desc: Learned mode predictor selects the best compression strategy based on task type and context.
pillar.intelligence.feature3Desc: Token, cost, and time budgets with SLO actions: warn, throttle, or block.

pillar.intelligence.feature9Desc: Every context item is scored by a six-factor potential function combining relevance, structure, recency, history, cost, and redundancy.

pillar.memory.headline: Every new session starts from zero. Your AI forgets everything it learned.
pillar.memory.solution: LeanCTX persists sessions, project knowledge, dependency graphs, and agent handoffs across restarts. The Session Survival Engine ensures structured recovery queries survive context compaction, so no critical context is lost mid-task. Facts are stored with confidence scores and automatically decay over time. Knowledge rooms organize information by topic, and structured handoff bundles allow seamless agent-to-agent transitions with full context preservation.

pillar.verification.title: Verification
pillar.verification.headline: You can't verify whether your AI's output is correct, complete, or safe.
pillar.verification.solution: LeanCTX produces verified outputs. Policy invariants are formally verified in Lean4 with 82 machine-checked theorems. Every context decision generates an auditable trail with pipeline metrics and provenance chains. Outputs are checked for valid paths, correct identifiers, and structural integrity. Claim-based verification decomposes proofs into atomic, verifiable units with Quality Levels 0-4.

pillar.verification.feature2Desc: ContextProofV2 decomposes verification into atomic claims. Each claim is routed to the appropriate verifier — from deterministic checks to Lean4 proofs.
pillar.verification.feature3Desc: Five assurance tiers: Provenance (Q0), Deterministic (Q1), Tested (Q2), Policy Proved (Q3), Formally Verified (Q4). Every output carries its exact trust level.
pillar.verification.feature4Desc: JSON and HTML proof reports with pipeline metrics, SLO snapshots, and provenance chains.
pillar.verification.feature5Desc: Path and identifier preservation as the quality gate mechanism. Structure verification with WARN/FAIL semantics ensures no valid paths or identifiers are lost during compression.
pillar.verification.feature6Desc: 4-layer compression engine with quality gate — formally proven: signatures mode preserves all exports, map mode preserves imports, aggressive mode leaks zero secrets. 82 Lean4 theorems, 0 sorry.
pillar.verification.feature7Desc: Deterministic sessions with replay hashes, CI gates, and regression detection.
pillar.verification.feature8Desc: State machine formally verified in Lean4. Terminal states are sinks, lifecycle ordering is monotonic, invalid envelopes are rejected.

pillar.contextBus.title: Context Bus
pillar.contextBus.headline: Context changes happen silently. No agent knows what another agent just learned, changed, or decided.
pillar.contextBus.solution: The Context Bus is a persistent, append-only event log with versioned events, causal lineage, consistency levels, and selective routing. Every session mutation, knowledge update, artifact creation, and tool call is published as a typed event with monotonic versioning. Agents subscribe with TopicFilters to receive only relevant events, send directed messages to specific agents, and use cursor-based polling or SSE for real-time updates. Cross-machine transport is supported via signed TransportEnvelopes and the Google A2A JSON-RPC protocol.
pillar.contextBus.feature1Desc: Agents subscribe with TopicFilters — filter by event kind, actor, consistency level, or agent identity. Directed events target specific agents only, reducing noise and saving tokens.
pillar.contextBus.feature2Desc: Each event carries a consistency level — local (informational), eventual (shared, async), or strong (requires sync) — so agents know which changes to prioritize.
pillar.contextBus.feature3Desc: TransportEnvelopeV1 wraps context packages and handoff bundles with HMAC-SHA256 signatures and agent identity for secure cross-machine transport. Send via CLI (lean-ctx pack send) or HTTP (/v1/a2a/handoff).
pillar.contextBus.feature4Desc: JSON-RPC 2.0 endpoint at /a2a supports tasks/send, tasks/get, and tasks/cancel. Agent Card published at /.well-known/agent.json for standard A2A discovery.
pillar.contextBus.feature5Desc: Full-text search over event payloads (FTS5), causal lineage graphs via parent_id chains, cursor-based replay from any point. Events survive server restarts. Automatic backfill from SQLite.
pillar.contextBus.problem: Agent A learns that the database schema changed. Agent B, working on the same project, has no idea and writes queries against the old schema. Without a shared event stream, context drift is invisible.

pillar.contextBus.metaDesc: Topic-filtered event routing, directed events, HMAC-signed cross-machine transport, Google A2A JSON-RPC compatibility, and FTS5 search. SSE streaming with automatic backfill.

docsConfiguration.configPriorityDesc: When the same setting is defined in multiple places, LeanCTX uses a clear priority order. Higher-priority sources override lower ones:
docsConfiguration.configPriorityTomlNote: Within a single config file, TOML is a key-value format — there is no line-order priority. If you define the same key twice, the TOML parser will use the last occurrence, but this is considered a syntax error. Use lean-ctx config validate to catch such issues.
docsConfiguration.commonConfusionDesc: LeanCTX has several parameters with "max" in their name that control completely different things. This table clarifies which parameter controls what:
docsConfiguration.confusionGraphIndexDes: Graph file scan limit — how many files the JSON graph index scans for dependency analysis. This is what lean-ctx gain shows as "Graph: N files".
docsConfiguration.confusionKnowledgeDesc: Knowledge facts — how many learned facts (from conversations) are stored per project. Has nothing to do with the graph.
docsConfiguration.confusionEmbeddingsDes: Embedding index — how many facts are indexed in the vector store for semantic search. Separate from knowledge facts.
docsConfiguration.confusionArchiveDiskDe: Archive storage — maximum disk space for zero-loss compression archives. Unrelated to memory or graph.
docsConfiguration.confusionArchiveAgeDes: Archive retention — how long archived tool results are kept before cleanup.
docsConfiguration.confusionStaleDaysDesc: Knowledge staleness — facts not accessed for this many days become eligible for pruning during consolidation. Does not delete instantly — facts are pruned only when auto_consolidate runs.
docsConfiguration.confusionCallout: Example: If lean-ctx gain shows "Graph: 2000 files (capped)" and you want more coverage, increase graph_index_max_files — not max_facts. max_facts controls knowledge memory, which is a completely separate system.
docsConfiguration.memoryLifecycleDesc: Memory entries (facts, patterns, gotchas) have a confidence score that changes over time:
docsConfiguration.memoryLifecycleStep1: New facts start with high confidence (based on source quality)
docsConfiguration.memoryLifecycleStep2: Daily decay (decay_rate) gradually reduces confidence of unused facts
docsConfiguration.memoryLifecycleStep3: Access resets — when a fact is recalled by the agent, its confidence is restored
docsConfiguration.memoryLifecycleStep5: Stale facts (not accessed for stale_days) become eligible for pruning
docsConfiguration.memoryLifecycleCallout: Safe to tune: Reducing stale_days from 30 to 7 means facts unused for a week are pruned sooner. This is safe — frequently accessed facts are never stale regardless of this setting. Increasing decay_rate from 0.01 to 0.05 makes facts lose confidence 5× faster, which is useful in fast-changing projects where old context quickly becomes irrelevant.
ce.title: What is Context Engineering? - LeanCTX
ce.metaDesc: Context engineering is the discipline of optimizing the full information environment an AI agent operates in — not just the prompt, but memory, compression, governance, and verification.
ce.heroDesc: It's the shift from prompt engineering to context operations — the discipline of designing, compressing, and governing the full information environment your AI agent works in. LeanCTX is that discipline, automated.
ce.problemDesc: Prompt engineering optimized the input. Context engineering optimizes the environment.
ce.problemP1: When AI agents were limited to single-turn interactions, prompt engineering was sufficient. You crafted the right instruction, the model returned a useful response, and the workflow ended.
ce.problemP2: Modern AI coding agents operate differently. They run multi-step workflows across dozens of files, maintain state across sessions, and make decisions that compound over time. The prompt is no longer the bottleneck — the context is.
ce.problemP3: A coding agent with a perfect prompt but poor context will hallucinate file paths, lose track of prior decisions, and repeat work it already completed. The failure mode isn't bad instructions — it's an incomplete picture of the codebase.
ce.frameworkDesc: Context engineering represents a fundamental change in how we think about AI agent inputs.
ce.shift1Desc: Instead of a fixed system prompt, context engineering builds a pipeline that assembles the right context for each task — reading only what's relevant, at the right compression level, with the right metadata.
ce.shift2Desc: Rather than hand-picking which files to include, context engineering reads each file's structure, keeps the parts that carry real signal, and compresses the rest — automatically.
ce.shift3Desc: Context engineering adds session memory, a knowledge graph, and clean handoffs, so agents build up understanding over time instead of starting from scratch every conversation.
ce.disciplineDesc: Context engineering spans four interconnected domains, each addressing a different aspect of the agent's information environment.
ce.domain1Title: Fit more signal into fewer tokens
ce.domain1Desc: Multiple read modes (full, map, signatures, entropy, aggressive), tree-sitter AST parsing across 18+ languages, and semantic chunking reduce file content by 60–99% while preserving the information agents need to make decisions.
ce.domain2Desc: Session snapshots, knowledge graphs, handoff ledgers, and prospective memory allow agents to recall prior decisions, avoid repeated work, and transfer context between team members or agent instances.
ce.domain3Desc: Role-based access policies, token budgets, SLO enforcement, and path sandboxing ensure agents operate within defined boundaries — reading only what they should, spending only what's allocated.
ce.domain4Desc: Output validation, proof artifacts, path and identifier preservation checks, and information-loss scoring give measurable confidence that compressed context retains the semantic content the agent requires.
ce.implDesc: LeanCTX is an open-source context engineering runtime that brings these principles into production for AI coding agents.
ce.implToolsDesc: A comprehensive tool surface for reading, searching, compressing, and managing context — all exposed via the Model Context Protocol.
ce.implReadModesDesc: From full cached reads to entropy-filtered compression, each mode is optimized for a specific task: editing, exploring, reviewing, or referencing.
ce.implShellDesc: Pattern-based compression for git, cargo, npm, docker, and other CLI output — reducing verbose command results to structured, token-efficient summaries.
ce.implLocalDesc: Runs entirely local. No telemetry, no cloud dependencies, no data leaving your machine. Open-source under Apache-2.0.
ce.ctaDesc: LeanCTX is free, open-source, and installs in under a minute. See what context engineering can do for your AI workflow.

docs.cortex.title: Context Engine
docs.cortex.metaDesc: How LeanCTX's Context Engine architecture enriches AI context with cross-source intelligence, relevance ranking, and active inference.
docs.cortex.introP1: The Context Engine is LeanCTX's intelligence layer that goes beyond simple file caching. It connects multiple data sources, ranks content by relevance, and proactively prefetches context your AI agent is likely to need next.
docs.cortex.introP2: Think of it as a search engine for your entire development context — code, issues, documentation, and external APIs — unified into a single query interface.
docs.cortex.pipelineStep1Desc: Content chunks from files, providers, and APIs are indexed with BM25 full-text search.
docs.cortex.pipelineStep2Desc: Cross-source edges connect related content (e.g., a GitHub issue mentioning a file path).
docs.cortex.pipelineStep3Desc: Saliency scoring combines recency, access frequency, and semantic relevance.
docs.cortex.pipelineStep4Desc: Active inference uses tool call patterns to prefetch context before you ask for it.
docs.cortex.crossSourceDesc: When you read a file, the Context Engine automatically surfaces related context from other sources. A ctx_read of auth.rs might append hints from a GitHub issue about JWT expiry or a Jira ticket about the authentication refactor.
docs.cortex.banditDesc: LeanCTX uses Thompson sampling to learn which providers deliver the most useful context for your workflow. Providers that consistently return relevant results get queried more often; noisy providers are automatically deprioritized.
docs.cortex.activeInferenceDesc: Based on your recent tool calls, the Context Engine predicts what context you'll need next and prefetches it in the background. If you just read auth.rs and middleware.rs, it might pre-query GitHub issues tagged with 'authentication'.

docs.budgets.title: Budgets, Roles & SLOs
docs.budgets.metaDesc: Configure token budgets, role-based limits, and SLO monitoring for LeanCTX sessions.
docs.budgets.intro: LeanCTX tracks token usage per session and provides two monitoring systems: Budget Warnings (role-based limits) and SLO Violations (service level objectives). Both help you stay aware of context consumption.
docs.budgets.warningDesc: A BudgetWarning event fires when your session token usage reaches 80% of the configured limit (default: 200,000 tokens → warning at ~160,000). This appears in the Observatory as budget · {role} tokens {percent}% WARNING.
docs.budgets.sloDesc: A separate SloViolation event fires when total session tokens exceed the SLO threshold (default: 200,000). This appears as violated · SessionContextTokens. Unlike BudgetWarning, SLOs are configured independently and can track additional metrics.
docs.budgets.differenceDesc: Both measure the same token counter but with different thresholds. BudgetWarning fires at 80% (early warning), while SessionContextTokens fires at 100% (actual violation).
docs.budgets.rolesDesc: Roles define budget limits. Create a file in ~/.lean-ctx/roles/ or <project>/.lean-ctx/roles/:
docs.budgets.sloConfigDesc: SLOs are defined in slos.toml (searched in ~/.lean-ctx/ and <project>/.lean-ctx/):
docs.budgets.resetDesc: Reset the token counter mid-session with ctx_session action=reset. Switch roles with ctx_session action=role value=<name> (also resets the budget). Reload SLOs after editing with ctx_session action=slo value=reload.
docs.budgets.blockingDesc: By default, budgets only warn (never block). To enable hard blocking, set block_at_percent = 100 in your role file. The default 255 means "never block".
docs.budgets.builtinDesc: LeanCTX ships with default roles: coder, reviewer, debugger, ops, admin. View the active role with ctx_session action=role.
